entries.title: White Sox still want the division title, but earning a playoff berth 'would be everything'
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> have grander ambitions than the third wild card spot, or even the American League Central title.</p><p>“If we get to do what we want to do, we’re going to be playing in the ALDS, CS and hopefully the World Series,” said Grant Taylor.</p><p>But assistant general manager Jin Wong was the White Sox executive accompanying the team for their road series in Kansas City on Tuesday. After a victory and a Rangers loss to the Mets lowered the White Sox' magic number for clinching a wild card berth to two entering Wednesday, Chris Getz and Josh Barfield flew into town to join him.</p><p>It doesn’t appear Getz is in town to deliver a postgame message to the team about the importance of staying focused on catching the Cleveland Guardians. The franchise’s first playoff appearance in five years is something to celebrate.</p><p>“It would be everything,” starter Davis Martin said of the Sox clinching a playoff spot. “We've been wrapped up in the division [race], and that's still something that's been our goal since the beginning. But from a standpoint of where we've been the last three years, just to be a part of something like that and to turn around and be the spark plug to something that maybe continues on for five, six, seven, eight years, it's just exciting.”</p><p>Martin is the longest-tenured player on the White Sox, which only means he’s been around since 2022, but plenty of suffering has been packed into that window of time. He can remember being asked “how do you sleep at night” in interviews in 2024, as if playing for a bad baseball team was a black mark on his life. Even friends and family asked if he’d rather just be traded, just to get away.</p><p>“I told all of them: my goal would be to be a part of the team that turns it around,” Martin told the Sun-Times. “To be in the situation we are now, which felt like a pipe dream two years ago, and now it’s sitting there looking at you in the face. It's incredible.”</p><p>There’s historical precedent for how incredible it is for the White Sox to make the playoffs at all. No team in MLB history has reached the postseason after three-consecutive 100-loss seasons, and the expanded playoff field can only do so much to blunt that accomplishment. But Sox players — when they’re not quoting their dire preseason projections — more sharply note the difference in how it <i>feels</i> to be part of this team, compared to just two years prior.</p><p>“In the beginning of the year, nobody really believed in us and what we are doing and now look at us,” said All-Star third baseman Miguel Vargas. “If we do it, it’s going to mean a lot for us. I think it’s a special moment.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable has been cherishing moments in places like Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City and Busch Stadium in St. Louis that lack prominent out-of-town scoreboards to distract his players, and himself. But on nights like Wednesday, where the result of Rangers-Mets could dictate whether it’s possible for the Sox to clinch a historic playoff berth, and the result of Guardians-Red Sox could mean there’s a chance to pull ahead in the AL Central, it’s hard not to get curious.</p><p>"It's been a challenge the last couple of weeks, honestly,” Venable said. “It's part of this. It's the position that we've earned, that we're in.”</p><p>It will also say a lot about what the Sox are doing in the visitor’s locker room after the game. Teams like the Dodgers or Yankees might celebrate a Wild Card spot with a polite champagne toast and a short speech about larger goals. A team like the White Sox, with their shared history, will go a different route.</p><p>“It’s not really our speed,” Martin said of a polite toast. “We kind of do everything full-go. I don’t expect it to be casual.”</p>

entries.title: Idaho authorities present new lead on Tylenol murders tied to recently identified man
entries.summary: <p>A recently identified Idaho man who died in 1982 — known as the “Unknown Wanderer” — could have ties to the four-decade-old Tylenol murders case, according to law enforcement agencies in Idaho.</p><p>Dr. Matthew Francis Betkouski died of cyanide poisoning in the pews of a Boise church in 1982, with $1,900 cash and recently dyed hair, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://adacounty.id.gov/sheriff/news/acso-solves-decades-old-unknown-wanderer-cold-case/" target="_blank" >Ada County sheriff’s office</a>.</p><p>The agency, which had been searching for the man's identity for decades, is being careful not to officially name Betkouski as a suspect in the murders even though Sheriff Matt Clifford announced evidence is going to be presented as part of an upcoming Roku documentary titled “Unmasking the Tylenol Killer” set to premiere Oct. 9.</p><p>The Ada County sheriff’s office is also sharing relevant evidence with Chicago police that may be connected to the murders.</p><p>“More information does exist in this case that we won’t be releasing today,” said Tim Cooper, a detective with the Ada County sheriff's office. “Our goal today is to generate leads in this case or others.”</p><p>Seven Chicago-area people died in September 1982 after ingesting cyanide-laced Tylenol. Johnson & Johnson recalled every form of the over-the-counter drug and created more tamper-proof pills and packaging as law enforcement searched for the culprit.</p><p>Chicago police Wednesday confirmed it had been in contact with the Ada County authorities regarding the case to “determine whether there is a connection to the Tylenol murders investigation, which remains an open cold case.”</p><p>James Lewis, a longtime leading suspect, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for extortion nearly a year later for demanding $1 million from Johnson & Johnson “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/metro-state/2023/7/10/23789606/james-lewis-prime-suspect-in-tylenol-tampering-cases-dead-at-76" target="_blank" ><u>to stop the killings</u></a>" and maintained his innocence until <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/10/23790603/tylenol-james-lewis-extortion-cyanide-mcnamee-chicago-obituary" target="_blank" >he died in 2023</a>.</p><div Lewis, the suspect in the 1982 Tylenol poisonings that killed seven people in the Chicago area and triggered a nationwide scare died in 2023. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>(Keith Myers/The Kansas City Star, distributed by the Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>No one has been charged in the case. </p><p>But the latest information could reveal new potential leads in the case.</p><p>Idaho investigators traced evidence — and eventually a DNA match — to Betkouski's brother after police positively identified the “Unknown Wanderer."</p><p>Betkouski struggled with mental illness throughout his life, though a traumatic brain injury in 1974 worsened his condition, investigators said. He wrote about his struggles with schizophrenia and depression, and that he was convinced a euphoria he gained from imagining scenes of violence could cure him.</p><p>Photos show him in Chicago in December 1981, though investigators couldn't place him in the city during the time of the murders.</p><p>In 1975, Betkouski, a chemist, moved to Jacksonville, Florida, for work, where he was reported by colleagues to management for talking about committing the “perfect crime” and suicide via cyanide, investigators said.</p><p>He was fired from Lockheed in 1982 for taking home unauthorized materials from the lab and over an “incident” at a local pharmacy in which he tried to obtain pills for an “experiment,” investigators said. A co-worker at the time reported him for allegedly saying poison could be slipped into pharmaceuticals.</p><p>A search of his childhood bedroom, where he stayed with his brother occasionally as an adult, turned up a map of Chicago made in the 1970s as well as a bottle of sodium cyanide — a different kind than was used in the Chicago area murders, investigators said. </p><p>Idaho investigators later connected with Arlington Heights police regarding their Tylenol murders cases. They also reached out to the Las Cruces Police Department in New Mexico, which also had unsolved cyanide poisoning in pharmaceuticals cases before the Chicago area murders.</p><p>Seven weeks before his death, Betkouski disappeared from his Las Cruces home. He then sold his car near the Mexico border shortly after and was subsequently found dead in the Boise church.</p><p>Chicago police ask that tips about the case be submitted to CPDTip.com or by calling 800-535-7867.</p><p>“This isn’t over, and what you’ve heard today could take months or years to work through,” Clifford said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/10/23790603/tylenol-james-lewis-extortion-cyanide-mcnamee-chicago-obituary" target="_blank" >Tylenol suspect James Lewis said anyone could have poisoned those capsules — then explained how</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2023/7/11/23790874/tylenol-killings-james-lewis-highland-park-chicago-unabomber-mcveigh-domestic-terrorism" target="_blank" >STEINBERG: Tylenol killings and the mystery of murder</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Alex Bregman ‘felt like I got hit by a baseball bat to the face,’ working to make quick return to Cubs
entries.summary: <p>Trust me, you don’t want to be <b>Alex Bregman</b> right now.</p><p>“I felt like I got hit by a baseball bat to the face, pretty much,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ third baseman said Wednesday, three days after he took a foul ball to the face while standing on deck during a game in Cincinnati.</p><p>Bregman and the Cubs have said they’ve received relative <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/22/cubs-alex-bregman-not-on-injured-list-regular-season-playoffs" >“great news” since</a>, in terms of a potential return, one that could come as soon as this weekend.</p><p>But while that would be a boost to the Cubs’ chances as they approach the most meaningful games of their season, he’s dealing with some significant aftereffects, with multiple facial fractures.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/T7ZbU-xz3UU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Alex Bregman on taking a baseball to the face"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“The pain’s been fine,” Bregman said. “I guess I fractured something right by the nerve in my face, so the whole left side of my face has been a little bit numb. As soon as the swelling goes down, I’m sure I’ll feel the breaks a little bit more.</p><p>“But all in all, I’m super lucky that it hit where it hit. A lot of gratitude, because if it was a few centimeters higher, it could have been detrimental.”</p><p>And here’s some more body horror:</p><p>“There’s a lot of fluid in my face,” Bregman said. “If I move, the fluid moves. If I’m bouncing up and down, my face feels like it’s bouncing up and down.”</p><p>All that is to illustrate what Bregman’s dealing with. But being the lauded hard-worker he is, it’s little surprise that he’s champing at the bit to get back in the lineup.</p><p>“[Tuesday] was brutal. I wanted to play,” he said. “I hope [to play this weekend]. We’ll see. One step at a time. I don’t know. I’m going to try to get in there [Wednesday].”</p><p>That last line was a joke, in case you were wondering. Bregman still has a lot to test out to see how he feels and how realistic such a quick comeback is.</p><p>“He’s doing well. But we’ve got to take some steps here,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “I’m excited how he feels, and he’s excited. But he still needs to feel some things. He hasn’t run around yet, and he’s got to do that. He’s got to know what it feels like.</p><p>“We’ve got to be careful, and we’ve got to go through the proper steps.”</p><h3><b>Bummer of a bunt</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> entered Wednesday with a .176 batting average in his last 18 games.</p><p>He got a chance to help produce a run in extra innings Tuesday, but he popped up a bunt attempt with two men on and nobody out in the 10th inning of an eventual 8-2 loss.</p><p>It’s a relative nit to pick from a game in which the Cubs went 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position, but with a lot on the line in the season’s final week, it could be among the moments that loom large.</p><p>“These are the moments you prepare for,” Shaw said. “I know that I’m going to have a situation again where I’m going to have to put a bunt down. We all know what the stakes are. All we can do is keep preparing for these moments.</p><p>“An experience like this is going to help the next time I’m in that situation, and that’s all you can walk away with.”</p><h3><b>Palencia back?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Since allowing seven runs in his first five outings after a lengthy IL stint, righty reliever <b>Daniel Palencia</b> hasn’t allowed an earned run in seven straight appearances, helpful as the Cubs look for their bullpen to stabilize before the postseason begins.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Struggling at the end of a great year, White Sox reliever Sean Newcomb feels he's gotten too predictable
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The <b>Sean Newcomb </b>fastball that Tigers infielder <b>Hao-Yu Lee</b> hit for a game-tying home run last Friday against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> sizzled in at 96.7 mph.</p><p>That was frustrating, but also answered a question for a reliever who has already logged 88 innings on the year.</p><p>“It’s not a stuff thing,” Newcomb told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Instead, Newcomb attributes a 10.80 ERA in September to becoming too predictable. His four-seam fastball has been one of the best pitches in the sport, but Lee homered on the fifth four-seamer of that at-bat.</p><p>Newcomb has struggled to land his slurve to get ahead in counts too, but feels this stretch resembles an earlier point of the season when he was getting beat on too many fastballs.</p><p>“The frustrating part is me not realizing it right away,” Newcomb said. “Pushing through it instead of taking a step back, looking at the big picture.”</p><h3><b>Opening jitters</b></h3><p>Before tossing two scoreless innings on Wednesday, Newcomb’s only scoreless appearance in September was also the only scoreless outing for a White Sox “opener” in their last four usages, as <b>Bryan Hudson</b> was touched up for four runs (three earned) on Wednesday night before giving way to <b>Erick Fedde</b>.</p><p>The Sox have prioritized handedness matchups in the first inning all season, with Wednesday being their MLB-leading 31st use of an opener, and show no signs of backing down.</p><p>“It's an approach that we feel strongly about, specifically with Fedde,” said manager Will Venable. “Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. But it's something we feel strongly gave us the best chance today.”</p>

entries.title: Kevin Gausman bangs up shoulder, Cubs lose another to Marlins: ‘The baseball gods are going to test you’
entries.summary: <p>If back-to-back losses with a chance to clinch a playoff spot weren’t frustrating enough for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>, here’s a new potential complication at the very end of the regular season.</p><p>Kevin Gausman – the righty pitcher who headlined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >Jed Hoyer’s trade-deadline haul</a> and figured to be a candidate to log significant playoff innings after helping the Blue Jays to the World Series last season – banged his left shoulder while making a diving play at third base in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s 3-2 loss to the Marlins. He exited the game with the trainer.</p><p>Is it a big deal? Something that could possibly impact his effectiveness or availability come the start of the postseason, just a few days away?</p><p>The best Gausman and the Cubs had Wednesday night after the game was that they’ll wait and see.</p><p>“I dislocated this shoulder in high school, a long time ago. I didn’t necessarily do the exact same thing, but I just kind of banged it good,” Gausman said. “I felt fine until I stood up to check the other runner, and it felt like the left shoulder was pretty weak at that point.</p><p>“It still feels pretty weak, but we’ll see how it feels tomorrow and get some treatment. Hopefully, it’s just a couple-day thing.</p><p>“I hope I wake up and feel great tomorrow. But you never know. I’ll get on some medicine and get some treatment, try to get in front of it tonight. It’s just a wait-and-see type thing.”</p><p>Though they hope it’s nothing serious, the Cubs can’t afford another pitching headache at the moment, not with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-red-sox-friday-doubleheader-boston-weather-forecast-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoffs-postseason" >nasty weather in Boston jumbling up their final series</a> of the regular season against the Red Sox this weekend. Those games – two of which will now be played in a Friday doubleheader – will be meaningful, with the NL wild-card standings bunched up and home-field advantage in the opening-round, best-of-three series up for grabs.</p><p>It’ll be challenging enough for the Cubs to get through the weekend, with its scheduling chaos, and set up their playoff rotation the way they want to. Anything limiting Gausman would make matters that much more complicated.</p><p>But the Cubs have to get to the playoffs first, still not something that seems unlikely; they’d have to lose all of their final four games, with the Diamondbacks winning their last four, to completely collapse and miss the postseason altogether.</p><p>That has been what’s happened in the first two games of the regular season’s final week, though, with the Cubs dropping each of the first two contests in a home series with the sub-.500 Marlins, an opponent that seemingly offered an opportunity to punch their playoff ticket, certainly when compared to this weekend’s foe, the playoff-bound Red Sox.</p><p>But the offense has gone as cold as the Wrigley Field conditions at a bad time, with the Cubs following up Tuesday’s 1-for-18 showing with runners in scoring position by going 1-for-8 in such situations Wednesday, Dansby Swanson’s broken-bat two-run single only briefly getting the Cubs out of trailing position before a video-reviewed double-play ball was flipped into an RBI ground out that gave the Marlins the lead for good in the next inning.</p><p>“It always seems like the baseball gods are going to test you, and it always seems to come at a time when you don’t want it to,” Gausman said. “But those are the things that are going to happen at this time of the year. It’s how you bounce back when those things do happen, when you get punched in the face.</p><p>“This group, since I’ve been here, has been resilient, and they were a lot before I was here. You can bank on those guys being ready to go.”</p>
